## My Reasoning

I've been farming in Quzhou my whole life. The land here on the North China Plain is flat and fertile, and there's really only one system that makes sense: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same ground. I've seen people try to get clever with cash crops — cotton, vegetables — and most of them regret it eventually. At 59, I'm not interested in risk. My body can still handle the work, but I'm not going to chase something unproven.

My concern this year, like every year, is groundwater. We've all watched the water table drop. The government's been pushing reduced irrigation, and they're right to. I try to keep my wheat down to three irrigations instead of the old four — jointing, grain-fill are the two I never skip; the winter water I give if it's dry enough to crack the topsoil. For maize I lean on the summer rains and only irrigate at pollination if it's really dry.

I hold 12 mu of contracted land. All of it goes into the wheat-maize rotation. I don't split off a vegetable plot — my wife manages a small kitchen garden, but that doesn't count as my operation.

For wheat I'm using Jimai 22 — it's an improved variety I trust, consistent yields, good lodging resistance. For maize I go hybrid, Xianyu 335, which has given me reliable results on this soil.

I do rotary tillage in October before wheat seeding to break up the maize stubble. For the maize in June, I drill directly into the wheat stubble — no-tillage saves fuel and keeps the soil from drying out in the summer heat.

Fertilizer: I had a soil test done two years ago and haven't seen reasons to think things have changed much. I apply roughly according to the county extension service's recommendations, maybe a touch less nitrogen than they suggest since I've been slightly over in past years and the lodging showed it.
